title: How laws are made
examples: Who is in charge of making new laws?
What happens after a law is proposed?
How do we know if a law passes?

explain.say: A proposal is an idea for a new law. Someone must suggest this idea first.
The next step is debate. People talk about the proposal and share their views.
After debate, the members must vote. A majority vote decides if the law passes.
Once a law passes, courts apply it. Judges use the established laws to make decisions.
For example, if a proposal suggests new rules for littering, that is the idea.
In everyday life, when a local council wants to change crossing times, they follow this process. They propose it, debate it, and vote on it.

faq.q: Who actually has the power to make laws in our country?
faq.a: The elected representatives in the legislature, like a parliament, have the main power to create laws. You might also ask who writes the laws, or where laws are debated.
asks: Which group of people makes the rules?

faq.q: What is the difference between a proposal and an actual law?
faq.a: A proposal is just an idea that has not been accepted yet. It must go through debate and voting to become a law. You could also ask what a bill is, or what legislation means.
asks: Is a proposal the same as a law?
What happens before a law exists?

faq.q: Does everyone get to vote on every single law?
faq.a: Generally, only the elected members of the governing body get to vote on the final law. The public can debate and influence the process, though. You might also ask who votes, or if the public votes.
asks: Can ordinary people vote on laws?

faq.q: What is the role of the courts in lawmaking?
faq.a: Courts do not make laws; they apply the laws that have already been made. Judges interpret existing laws when people have disagreements. You could also ask what judges do, or how courts use laws.
asks: What do courts do with laws?

faq.q: What happens if the debate is very heated?
faq.a: The debate is a formal discussion where different sides present arguments for and against the proposal. The goal is to reach a clear understanding before a vote. You might ask about disagreements, or how arguments are presented.
asks: Can people argue a lot during debate?
What is the purpose of the discussion?

facts: Laws usually start as a proposal put forward by someone.
Debate allows people to discuss the good and bad points of an idea.
A majority vote is needed for a proposal to become a law.
Courts interpret and apply the laws that have already been passed.

quiz.say: An idea for a new rule is called a:
quiz.why: A proposal is the starting idea that needs to be discussed.

wrong.0: A vote is the action taken to decide on the idea.
wrong.2: A law is the final, accepted rule, not the initial idea.
wrong.3: Debate is the discussion about the idea, not the idea itself.

quiz.say: If a law is already in place, who decides if someone broke it?
quiz.why: Courts are the bodies responsible for applying existing rules to cases.

wrong.1: The person who suggested the idea does not enforce the law.
wrong.2: Debaters discuss ideas; they do not judge actions.
wrong.3: Voters decide if the law passes, but courts enforce it.

quiz.say: A proposal must first go through which stage before a vote can happen?
quiz.why: The debate is the necessary discussion period after a proposal is made.

wrong.0: Voting usually happens after a period of discussion.
wrong.1: Writing the proposal is the start; debate follows it.
wrong.3: Applying the law happens after the law is already established.
